prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice that allows many atoms to be interrogated without a trapping-light shift, and its experimental development to uncertainties near 10^-18, which has enabled laboratory tests of gravitational redshift and fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B002 as a single prize part with Katori and Ye, and my position is firmer than in round 1 because the first-round exchange answered most of what I had left open. The decisive test for me is whether the original experiment is identifiable and verified. The new content is a many-atom lattice in which the clock transition is not shifted by the trapping light, followed by independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) reaching agreement near 10^-18. That is a tool that opened a door to measurements nobody could make before: millimetre-scale redshift, comparisons that constrain varying constants, and dark-matter searches. In answer to the chair's question on discovery versus technique, I judge that the statutes allow an invention that demonstrably changes what can be observed, and this one has been used, not only demonstrated. In answer to the question on the citation, it should rest on the demonstrated accuracy, the redshift measurement and the fundamental-physics tests, and should not depend on a redefinition of the second that has not happened. I would add no second achievement. No candidate on the shortlist currently combines a mature, verified result with a credit set I could defend as the people who did the original work, and a weaker second part would dilute a clean first one.
statement.case_against: Two reservations remain and I will not hide them. First, priority: I have not seen the early-2000s papers in this file, so I am relying on memory that Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium lattice clock, with Ye's group following quickly and then taking the systematic uncertainty and stability much further, and that Lemonde and colleagues discussed related ideas in parallel. My own rule says the prize goes to the original experiment and not to the later, more spectacular one. I believe the pair is defensible because Katori's proposal and first demonstration and Ye's decisive experimental development are both original contributions to a single verified result. But the secretariat should check the chronology before the citation is fixed. Second, lineage with 2005 (Hall, Haensch, with Ye as a co-worker in the frequency-comb field) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche): the citation has to name the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice and not clocks or combs in general. A third point is that Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb community are not credited, which the committee should accept openly given the limit of three names.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B002 first, regards the magic-wavelength lattice as the concrete new idea, and says she has not independently checked how far parallel proposals overlapped. In round 1 I pressed the same chronology, and the chair has asked whether she and Kroll can report on it.
responses.response: I accept your science and I now think the chronology question is the only item that could change the credited pair, so I ask you and Stefan to say plainly what you can confirm: the date of Katori's proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, and the dates of the first independent demonstrations at JILA and in Paris. If you find that parallel work preceded Katori's, then the citation wording and perhaps the pair would need discussion. If you find what I recall, which is that Katori's proposal and first lattice clock came first and Ye's group followed independently, I think the pair is correct. I would draft the citation around the lattice concept and the accuracy it made possible, and I would drop any language that sounds like a prize for the best clock.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B002 low because of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and he prefers KPZ (B056), which he calls compact, mature and conceptually central. He concedes that Parisi and the exact-solution authors are outside the credited names and that his was the only opening ballot to place B056.
responses.response: I cannot accept the overlap argument as stated. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb as a ruler for optical frequency and the 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped ions and photons. A lattice clock interrogates many neutral atoms at once with the light shift cancelled, which is a different idea and has been verified separately. Ye shared the 2005 prize, but the question is what this work is for, not who he is. I take your discovery-versus-technique concern seriously and it is why the citation must name the new regime. On KPZ I remain unable to tell whether Takeuchi's liquid-crystal work is the original experimental confirmation, and the chair's summary notes that Kroll and Lindroth question reproduction beyond one system. With the credited names also omitting Parisi and the exact solutions, I do not think B056 meets the standard of identifying the people who did the original work, so I will not move to it, though I respect the conceptual case.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B015) as a verified new state of matter, argues that the experiment (Molenkamp's HgTe edge conduction) and theory (Kane and Mele) both exist and are reproduced, and concedes that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D contributors lie outside the three names.
responses.response: I agree the physics is verified and that the experimental observation in HgTe is the kind of original experiment I look for. My difficulty is the same one you name. The observation in HgTe rested on a proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, the 3D case belongs to Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Hasan and Cava, and Zhang is deceased. If I try to write a three-name citation I cannot say that those three did the original work without leaving out people whose contributions were as decisive. I also see the 2016 lineage. For me a new state of matter is not automatically better than a new measurement capability, and the credit is what separates them here. If the committee finds a defensible way to credit the quantum spin Hall effect alone, with prediction and observation, I would reconsider B015, but I do not see it from the record we have and I did not rank it above seventh at the opening.

responses.point: Pearce moved B002 ahead of IceCube (B043), says the clock may read as technology and not as a discovery about nature, and relies on Lindroth and Kroll for the priority questions. He says that if the committee wants a first-of-its-kind discovery, B043 is the stronger statement.
responses.response: I answered your technology question in round 1 and I stay with it. An invention that makes a previously unseeable phenomenon measurable and is then used to measure it qualifies, and the clocks have been so used. On B043, I agree that the diffuse flux is a real discovery. Where we differ is timing and credit. Only a handful of sources are identified, and the credit among Halzen, Spiering and the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers has not been settled in the file. I do not think waiting a few years costs the committee anything, because the result will not be superseded, and it gains source identification and a clearer credit record. I keep B043 as my first alternative and not as a rival, and I would be glad if you would tell us what the IceCube record shows about who built the detector concept.

responses.point: Danielsson moved the Higgs experiments (B053) down from first only because of attribution, and says that by doing so he may be choosing the comfortable prize over the important one. He regards Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as a defensible founder trio but concedes that he has not verified this.
responses.response: I do not read your move as choosing the comfortable prize. The merit is not in doubt, and I said so in round 1. My objection is statutory. Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee led the projects, and I have no evidence in the file that they carried out the decisive 2012 measurement or that three people can stand for two collaborations of thousands. A prize that names them would honour direction and not the original experiment. If you have a documented argument for why these three, tell us. Otherwise I would not put B053 into the preferred configuration, and I do not think the committee should treat the importance of the discovery as a substitute for a credible credit. I also note the 2013 prize recognised the mechanism, so the experiment may deserve its own recognition on another day, if a defensible credit can be written.

uncertainties: The chronology and priority of the magic-wavelength lattice proposal and of the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori, Ye, Lemonde and others) is still not confirmed against the original papers in this exchange, and could change the citation wording or the pair.

Whether the committee will accept that the many-atom lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think it is, but Mehlig, Pearce and others do not yet agree, and the committee has not written one agreed sentence of difference.
Whether B002 alone is the whole prize. I see no second shortlisted achievement with both maturity and a defensible credit, but I may be too strict on attribution for B015, B038 and B043.
How soon source identification and the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA credit will allow B043, and whether the pairing mechanism and Cao's role will allow B038 to be credited.
statement.conflict_note: I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and have long-running exchanges with its community, and Katori is at the University of Tokyo, so there is a possible institutional connection to my preferred configuration. I know of no personal collaboration, joint publication or funding link with Katori or Ye, and I will not take part in drafting the citation sentence about Katori if the committee judges the connection material. I also have ties to the Tohoku microscopy community (relevant to B025), and my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is on the committee, but no shortlisted candidate is from Chalmers. That Johansson and I also share an institution has no bearing on this configuration.
